stories.title: Nepal races to rescue 100 workers trapped in a tunnel as China halts Tibet operation
stories.summary: More than 100 people remain trapped in a hydropower tunnel in Nepal, while rescuers across the border in Tibet have been forced to withdraw as fears grow of renewed flooding. Nepali army helicopters were working on Friday to rescue more than 100 people trapped inside a hydropower tunnel after catastrophic floods devastated the country's northern border region. The army has already rescued 350 workers and local residents from the tunnel at the Upper Trishuli hydropower project in Rasuwa, according to the prime minister's office. Nepal Army spokesman Raja Ram Basnet said two helicopters had been dispatched but rescuers were facing difficult conditions, including problems locating entrances to the tunnel. "Our focus is in search and rescue of people," Basnet told AFP, adding that relief supplies were also being provided to survivors. The operation comes two days after a glacial collapse triggered a vast flow of ice, rock and debris through river valleys near Nepal's border with China's Tibet region. The US Geological Survey said the debris flow and flooding travelled nearly 100 kilometres along the Trishuli and Bhote Koshi rivers, destroying buildings and infrastructure and cutting a vital highway linking Nepal and China. The scale of the destruction was still emerging on Friday, with roads, bridges and several hydropower projects damaged or destroyed. Survivors described floodwaters sweeping through worksites with extraordinary speed. "There were at least 400 workers at the site," Dev Shrestha, who was airlifted from another hydropower project, told AFP. "More people died than were rescued." Worker Buddha Tamang said he survived because he was inside a tunnel when the flood struck.

stories.title: Weather tracker: More extreme rain in Japan and a tornado in France
stories.summary: Flash flooding and mudslides in Ishikawa and Toyama prefectures, while convective storms hit western Europe Following an “unprecedented” deluge in Chiba in mid-August, Japan has had more extreme rainfall in recent days. Moisture from the Sea of Japan brought relentless heavy rain to the prefectures of Ishikawa and Toyama on Thursday. In Himi, Toyama, 361.5mm of rain fell in 24 hours, equivalent to half the average annual rainfall in London and Paris. As a result of the downpours, several rivers burst their banks, leading to flash floods and mudslides with trees felled and buildings damaged. Japan’s Meteorological Agency issued its highest-level rain warning within the two prefectures earlier

stories.title: Dos Santos and Russell set world records in ‘crazy’ Zurich Diamond League
stories.summary: Dos Santos stormed to victory to set new men’s 400m hurdles time, while Russell broke women’s 100m hurdles record. Alison Dos Santos and Masai Russell each set a world record while Armand “Mondo” Duplantis won a historic pole vault in a barmy night of track and field in Zurich that would have more than pleased onlooking World Athletics President Sebastian Coe. “I expect the Olympic Games in two hours,” Coe said of his expectations of the penultimate Diamond League meet of the season on Thursday. The Swiss city’s Letzigrund Stadium had a raucous sellout 25,000 crowd and the still, balmy weather conditions helped no end for a heady night of athletics. Brazil’s Dos Santos was first up, clocking a sensational 45.80 seconds to beat the previous mark of 45.94 seconds set by Norway’s Karsten Warholm when winning gold at the Tokyo Olympics. “I have been showing great form throughout the season – that I am fast, I am strong,” said a confident Dos Santos, with Warholm finishing second and dubbing their discipline a “crazy event”. “As soon as I knew I was coming here, I was excited. The weather’s good, the track’s amazing,” the Brazilian added. Then came Russell, the Olympic champion of the US at 12.09 seconds to beat the previous best of 12.12 seconds set by Nigeria’s Tobi Amusan at the Eugene world championships in 2022. Both Dos Santos and Russell will leave Zurich with a cheque each for $80,000 for having broken their respective records. The world records were punctuated by a scintillating competition in the pole vault, eventually won by double Olympic and triple world champion Duplantis. The United States-born Swede came under real pressure from Greek rival Emmanouil Karalis, who vaulted a personal best of 6.20 metres.
